overview: Rozvi power grew in the late seventeenth century and became influential across the Zimbabwe plateau. Its rulers took over older political and settlement landscapes. The map’s 1650 start is earlier than that rise, and its 1815 endpoint precedes the major nineteenth-century breakup.

periods.title: Older centres and emerging leaders
periods.summary: Earlier Torwa settlements preceded the consolidation of Rozvi power.

periods.title: Rozvi regional power
periods.summary: Changamire rulers linked military authority with cattle, farming and regional exchange.

periods.title: Breakup and continuing resistance
periods.summary: Warfare and shifting alliances dismantled central power; resistance and local communities continued.

sections.title: A changing kingdom in an older landscape

items.text: Archaeology shows that the foundations at Danamombe, Naletale and Zinjanja predate Rozvi rule. Their later political importance should not make all the earlier builders disappear from the story. A new dynasty could inhabit and reinterpret an existing place.

Changamire Dombo’s campaigns challenged Portuguese positions in the late 1600s. Later Rozvi authority also depended on relationships with local rulers, rather than one ruler personally administering every settlement inside a solid map colour.

The economy rested heavily on cattle and crops, including millet and sorghum. Gold and ivory also entered exchange networks. A kingdom remembered for warfare still needed people tending herds and bringing in harvests.

Trade through Zumbo continued despite conflict with Portuguese interests. African traders carried goods between the interior and border markets, so excluding particular foreign merchants did not necessarily end long-distance exchange.

Naletale’s walls use carefully placed granite without mortar. Herringbone, chevrons, checks and contrasting stone create different patterns. The walls display planning and workmanship as well as separating and supporting parts of a settlement.

Nearby Nsalansala has decoration on the inside of its stone enclosure. This detail changes how we imagine the buildings: some carefully arranged patterns were intended for people within the space, not only for someone approaching from outside.

Ancient mines and finds such as metal bangles, needles and spearheads reveal another side of the Naletale landscape. Mineral extraction, metalworking and exchange accompanied the construction of its elaborate stone centres.

At Danamombe, excavators found a spindle whorl, a tool associated with spinning thread, alongside pottery and other household material. Such finds bring textile work into a history often illustrated mainly with walls and weapons.

Another Danamombe excavation recovered a mbira key. It is a small surviving part of a musical instrument, a reminder that sound and performance belonged to these settlements even though most of the music itself cannot be excavated.

Layered house floors, ash, charcoal, grinding equipment and animal remains help reconstruct repeated occupation. These materials do not all date to one reign, so a particular object cannot automatically be assigned to a named Rozvi king.

Rozvi oral narratives connect named hills, buildings and other places with ancestors and royal power. The authors of a recent study argue that these narratives should be tested alongside excavation evidence, while recognizing that places can carry several competing memories.

A modern recorded Shona form is “varozvi”, glossed as “destroyers” in the archaeological study. It helps explain the historical name, but this printed transcription is not a surviving inscription from Dombo’s reign. No securely checked contemporary indigenous written sentence is reproduced here.

ending.text: In the nineteenth century, internal disputes and incoming armies broke apart central Rozvi power. Some leaders continued resistance, while others and their communities entered new political relationships. Rozvi identities and traditions survived the state’s fragmentation.
